title: The rocket killed by one number
caption:
Europe's brand-new rocket blew itself up 37 seconds after liftoff because one number was too big. 🚀
Reused code squeezed the sideways speed from a 64-bit number into a 16-bit integer, which can't hold more than 32,767. The faster rocket overflowed it and both guidance computers crashed.
Should you ever reuse old code on new hardware? Defend your answer.
first_comment: The backup computer ran the exact same code, so it crashed the exact same way. Redundancy speedrun 💀
sources: ESA/CNES Inquiry Board report, 'Ariane 5 Flight 501 Failure' (J. L. Lions, July 1996): software reused from Ariane 4 converted the horizontal velocity bias (BH) from a 64-bit floating point number to a 16-bit signed integer; the larger values of Ariane 5 caused an operand error; the active and backup inertial reference systems, running identical software, both failed; the nozzles were commanded to full deflection, the launcher broke up and self-destructed about 37-40 seconds after lift-off on 4 June 1996
ESA: the four Cluster science satellites were lost on flight 501
